signals.title: Georgia Merritt stages contemporary design show at London antiques dealer
signals.description: Emerging designer Georgia Merritt has unveiled Refrain, an east London exhibition of sculptural furniture pieces informed by 18th-century architectural mouldings and musical staves. Refrain is the second solo show for Merritt , who was featured in our London Design Festival Dezeen Dispatch lineup of London's rising stars . Refrain is Georgia Merritt's second solo design show staged at antiques dealer M Kardana The exhibition brings together five of Merritt's pieces arranged across M Kardana , a 20th-century antiques shop on Hackney Road that was stripped back to form a gallery setting to accommodate the works. "My pieces can be read as furniture, but equally as sculptures, or propositions for an interior," Merritt told Dezeen. "Showing them at M Kardana, within the context of an antiques dealer, plays on that ambiguity." The exhibition includes a mirror that reveals Merritt's faux marble technique The design of each of Merritt's pieces was rooted in the inspiration she finds in the precision of both musical notation and architecture. Among them is a slim, wall-mounted mirror flanked by a duo of black lacquered doors that open out on full-length piano hinges. A floor lamp was topped with layers of organza Although made of birchwood, the doors look as if they are solid stone thanks to Merritt's distinctive painting technique, which involves hand-painting timber to create trompe l'œil faux marble furniture. The designer developed the granular process during a gilding apprenticeship that she completed when struggling to find work as a fine art graduate in 2020. Underscore is a wooden bench supported by a single leg Also on display is a delicate, hand-formed wire lamp encased in an ellipsoid shade made of silk organza overlaid with gazar. The lamp and its shade were positioned atop a stainless steel frame fitted with a central, rectilinear tray. Underscore is a sweeping bench supported by a single leg at one end, and resting against a wall at the other. The curved seating was carved from smooth sapele wood. Merritt wanted to visually interpret a glissando , the musical term for sliding from one note to the next. An low-slung table was topped with a textile canopy "The bench's profile recalls both Georgian architectural mouldings and the parallel lines of a musical stave," said the designer. A glass tablet was fitted atop the furniture's single leg, which was selected to echo a magnifying glass or other "apparatus for observation or examination". Merritt's fourth piece is a low-slung glass table, topped with an elongated canopy made of ivory silk that was clamped to the upper panes of glass with stainless-steel arms. Read: How London designers are making it work The final piece in the exhibition is another wall-mounted mirror fastened with piano hinges, but this one is full length and finished entirely in black lacquer. "When closed, the mirror's doors form a monolithic, modernist silhouette," said Merritt. Another all-black mirror features in the exhibition Refrain marks the second show that the designer has presented at M Kardana, following her Vague Precision exhibition in 2023. The designer considered how her practice, which she defines as art as much as design, has developed in recent years. "I think I'm continually working towards expressing something that I can sense quite clearly but can't necessarily define," she said. "With this exhibition, I feel a little closer to it." Merritt is interested in making pieces with an "ability to move between different contexts, whether that's a gallery, a domestic interior, or somewhere else". "I like the idea that their identity might shift slightly depending on where they're placed," she said. The designer was among the creatives showing in the Max Radford Gallery presentation at London's Collect fair in February. The photography is by Tazy Jessett Nash . Refrain is on display at M Kardana , 188A Hackney Road, London E2 7QL, United Kingdom, from 9 to 31 October 2026. visualFeast.title: Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
visualFeast.description: New York architect Diana Kellogg has renovated her historic Tribeca residence, highlighting materials repurposed from its industrial past. Kellogg and her family have occupied the home on Staple Street for 25 years, which is close to the studio that the architect shares with her filmmaker husband. Diana Kellogg has updated her home gradually over time, while retaining its industrial character The building originally served as cold storage for neighbouring produce distribution facilities, then became a plumber's supply storefront and eventually a residence around 50 years ago. Kellogg has renovated and updated the structure gradually over the years, and when her kids moved out, she decided to undertake a more comprehensive overhaul. Many of the built-in elements are formed from the salvage of the building's freight elevator An old freight elevator was removed and replaced with a space that Kellogg refers to as the Green Room. The glass-wrapped nook is lined with cushioned seating and used for intimate catch-ups over drinks, or private video calls. The kitchen similarly utilises salvaged elements The salvage from the elevator and other elements around the building were repurposed to create structures for the kitchen, bookcases, and a staircase that connects the four levels. "Throughout the house there were old glass and steel doors, and windows and stuff," Kellogg said. "I just moved them around and repurposed them." A space dubbed the Green Room is used for catch-ups and Zoom calls In keeping with the architecture, the decor remains industrial and spare, highlighting key elements like the fireplace and the 25-foot-long chestnut beams that span the ceiling. "It was a massive pain in the neck to strip those, but one of the best decisions we made, because they add so much warmth and character," said Kellogg. A steel staircase connects the home's four levels During the most recent renovation, the upstairs bedrooms with vaulted brick ceilings were reconfigured as neutrally decorated spaces separated by sliding mahogany doors. On the ground floor, the children's former playroom – complete with climbing ropes and a swing – was converted into a comfortable TV room, featuring a large L-shaped sofa and a variety of midcentury furniture pieces. The ground-floor children's playroom was recently converted into a media room Matching those on the level above, Noguchi pendant lights hang from the steel beams that Kellogg added to suspend the "jungle gym". "There's still one climbing rope down there that people think is an art piece, which I love," she said. Read: Crina Arghirescu Rogard adds "eccentric design" to historic penthouse in Tribeca Key artworks include a pair of photographs by Ljubodrag Andric , which he produced to sit either side of the first-floor fireplace and "give the place so much depth and warmth," said Kellogg. Downstairs, the walls are adorned with images of The Rajkumari Ratnavati Girl's School that Kellogg completed in 2021 in India's Thar Desert. Upstairs bedrooms are divided by mahogany sliding doors The roof terrace was relandscaped with planters and a variety of wooden outdoor furniture that forms dining and seating areas with views of a historic bridge between the adjacent buildings. "I really wanted an oasis up there, and to have it be a second living room," said Kellogg. "And there's the fabulous bridge, which we have kind of great views of from our house – which is, in my opinion, better than actually being inside it." The roof terrace was also refurbished with planters and outdoor furniture Many of Tribeca's former industrial buildings are now residential, housing large lofts and penthouses, while others contain galleries and creative spaces. Examples of other homes in the neighbourhood include a penthouse in the American Thread Building updated by Crina Arghirescu Rogard and a loft that Andrea Leung renovated to conceal "secret spaces". The photography is by Andrew Brinka . The post Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials appeared first on Dezeen .

visualFeast.title: Historic town hall in Limoges set on fire during French protests
visualFeast.description: Significant parts of the 143-year-old Limoges Town Hall in France have been destroyed in an arson attack, as protests broke out across the country over the weekend. On 17th October, Limoges Town Hall was set on fire. Videos taken by people on the ground show its slate roofs ablaze and its central bell tower collapsing. Officials have not yet confirmed the state of the town hall and whether the rest of the building is at risk of collapse, according to the BBC . Designed by French architect Charles-Alfred Leclerc, the neo-Renaissance Limoges Town Hall was built in 1883 and was listed as a historical monument in 1975. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sky News (@skynews) The neo-Renaissance Limoges Town Hall has been damaged in a fire An estimated 550,000 people in France took to the streets over the weekend to protest the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. Some demonstrations turned to violence and disorder, with hundreds of shops being looted and destroyed. Around 2,400 people have been arrested . Read: Huge fire breaks out at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris In addition to Limoges Town Hall, other buildings in France were set on fire in arson attacks, including a tourist office in Lyon . The mayor of Limoges has demanded a "Notre-Dame plan" to restore the town hall. A huge fire broke out at the iconic Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in 2019, which saw the Gothic landmark's 90-metre-high spire and parts of the roof collapse. After five years of reconstruction work, the cathedral reopened in 2024 with restored interiors and the spire rebuilt as a replica of the 1859 version lost to the fire. The top photo of Limoges Town Hall before the fire is by Sergey Dzyuba via Shutterstock. The post Historic town hall in Limoges set on fire during French protests appeared first on Dezeen .
